steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a computer vision paper presenting DGC-GNN, a graph neural network for 2D-3D matching that does not use visual descriptors. Cover how 2D-3D matching is done today, the problems with descriptor-based methods, recent descriptor-free work like GoMatch and its limits, our idea of using geometry and color cues, and a list of contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- 2D-3D matching: applications and traditional descriptor-based pipelines
- Drawbacks of storing descriptors; existing remedies
- Descriptor-free matching and GoMatch; its limitations
- Two questions: is geometry enough, and how to use it? Color cues
- DGC-GNN and contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- 2D-3D matching
  - key for visual localization (cite), 3D reconstruction (cite), SLAM (cite)
  - traditional: keypoints + descriptors from query image, exhaustive 2D-3D descriptor matching
  - cheaper: some approaches (cite) first use image retrieval (cite) to find similar database images, then descriptor-based image matching (cite) query vs retrieved
  - 2D-3D correspondences via 2D-2D matches + prebuilt 2D-3D correspondences in database
  - another approach (cite): search all point descriptors with efficient vocabulary-based method
  - Sattler et al. (cite): combine 2D-3D and 3D-2D search, active correspondence search -> faster, more efficient
- Drawbacks of descriptors
  - SOTA accuracy, but store high-dimensional descriptors per point in large point clouds
  - storage orders of magnitude more than point cloud + images (cite)
  - privacy attacks (cite); expensive maintenance, descriptor updates (cite) when adding descriptors/points
  - remedies: Yang et al. (cite) learned point selection for scene compression; methods (cite) learn 2D pixel -> 3D coordinate map, no explicit 3D scene; another work (cite) adversarial learning for content-concealing descriptors
- Descriptor-free matching
  - researchers (cite): deep learning for cross-domain direct 2D-3D matching and pose estimation without descriptors; differentiable geometric optimization
  - GoMatch (cite): significant progress, reasonable matching on real-world datasets (cite)
  - keypoints + 3D points -> bearing vectors in camera coordinate system; attention mechanism (cite)
  - still lags far behind descriptor-based methods (cite)
  - geometric cues only from points + local neighbors -> can't distinguish geometrically similar structures
- Two questions
  - (1) is geometry the only info? (2) how to use geometric info from points?
  - humans: global structure + local geometric cues; Fig. 1: locate building by structure, then local roof structure
  - visual context: color per point also constrains matching
  - still privacy-preserving: RGB of sparse keypoints insufficient to reconstruct scene
- DGC-GNN
  - graph-based, builds on GoMatch, geometric + color cues, global-to-local, descriptor-free
  - encodes position + RGB per point; global distance-angular embedding guides local matching
  - cluster-based transformer, inspired by earlier work (cite), limits information flow to local clusters
  - real-world data: more correct matches, more accurate pose; doubles GoMatch accuracy -> narrows gap
- Contributions
  - descriptor-free global-to-local GNN; multiple cues; progressive clustering module; accurate sparse matching, low memory, privacy-preserving, low maintenance cost
  - color per point crucial; RGB encoding -> significant gains
  - experiments: outperforms previous methods by large margin on matching and visual localization

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Establishing 2D-3D matches is very important in many computer vision applications, including visual localization, 3D reconstruction, and Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM). The traditional methods for point-to-point matches extract keypoints and descriptors from a query image and then match the 2D and 3D descriptors with exhaustive search. To avoid this computationally expensive matching process, some approaches make the search space smaller by first using image retrieval methods to find the most similar images in the database, and then they do descriptor-based image matching between the query and the retrieved images. Then the 2D-3D correspondences are established by connecting the 2D-2D image matches with the 2D-3D correspondences that are prebuilt in the database. Another approach builds 2D-to-3D matches by searching through all the point descriptors with an efficient vocabulary-based method. Sattler et al. also explore combining 2D-3D and 3D-2D search as an active correspondence search step, so the matching process is faster and more efficient.

Descriptor-based algorithms achieve state-of-the-art accuracy, but they have to store and maintain high-dimensional visual descriptors for each point in 3D point clouds that can be large. The stored model often needs orders of magnitude more storage than the point cloud and the images alone. These methods are also susceptible to privacy attacks, and they need computationally expensive model maintenance and descriptor update procedures when new descriptors or points are added to the model. Several approaches have been proposed for these limitations. Yang et al. use learned point selection to sample a subset of the point cloud and compress the scene. Other methods directly learn a function mapping 2D pixels to 3D coordinates, without storing the 3D scene explicitly. Also, another work introduces an adversarial learning framework to develop content-concealing descriptors that prevent privacy leakage.

- Descriptor-free matching
  - recent deep learning work: direct 2D-3D matching and pose estimation without descriptors, differentiable geometric optimization
  - GoMatch: big step, reasonable results on real-world datasets
  - keypoints + 3D points -> bearing vectors in camera frame; attention mechanism for correspondences
  - still far behind descriptor-based methods
  - only local geometric cues -> can't tell geometrically similar structures apart
- Two questions
  - (1) is geometry the only info? (2) how to use geometric info for matching?
  - humans: global structure + local cues; Fig. 1 building, then roof
  - color per point also constrains matching; sparse keypoint RGB can't reconstruct scene -> privacy kept
- DGC-GNN
  - graph-based, global-to-local, geometric + color cues; builds on GoMatch
  - position + RGB encoding; global distance-angular embedding; cluster-based transformer
  - more correct matches, better pose; doubles GoMatch accuracy
- Contributions
  - descriptor-free global-to-local GNN with progressive clustering; low memory, privacy-preserving, low maintenance cost
  - color is crucial; RGB encoding gives significant gains
  - outperforms previous methods by large margin on matching and visual localization

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Establishing 2D-3D matches is very important in many computer vision applications, including visual localization, 3D reconstruction, and Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM). The traditional methods for point-to-point matches extract keypoints and descriptors from a query image and then match the 2D and 3D descriptors with exhaustive search. To avoid this computationally expensive matching process, some approaches make the search space smaller by first using image retrieval methods to find the most similar images in the database, and then they do descriptor-based image matching between the query and the retrieved images. Then the 2D-3D correspondences are established by connecting the 2D-2D image matches with the 2D-3D correspondences that are prebuilt in the database. Another approach builds 2D-to-3D matches by searching through all the point descriptors with an efficient vocabulary-based method. Sattler et al. also explore combining 2D-3D and 3D-2D search as an active correspondence search step, so the matching process is faster and more efficient.

Descriptor-based algorithms achieve state-of-the-art accuracy, but they have to store and maintain high-dimensional visual descriptors for each point in 3D point clouds that can be large. The stored model often needs orders of magnitude more storage than the point cloud and the images alone. These methods are also susceptible to privacy attacks, and they need computationally expensive model maintenance and descriptor update procedures when new descriptors or points are added to the model. Several approaches have been proposed for these limitations. Yang et al. use learned point selection to sample a subset of the point cloud and compress the scene. Other methods directly learn a function mapping 2D pixels to 3D coordinates, without storing the 3D scene explicitly. Also, another work introduces an adversarial learning framework to develop content-concealing descriptors that prevent privacy leakage.

Recently researchers started to explore deep learning techniques for cross-domain direct 2D-3D matching and pose estimation without visual descriptors, and they show that descriptor-free matching is possible through differentiable geometric optimization. The recent GoMatch is significant progress in descriptor-free 2D-3D keypoints matching, and it gets reasonable matching performance on several real-world datasets. GoMatch first finds keypoints in the query image, and these keypoints and the 3D points from the model are converted to bearing vectors in the camera coordinate system. Then it uses an attention mechanism to establish reliable 2D-3D correspondences. GoMatch gets reasonable accuracy, but its performance is still a lot worse than the descriptor-based methods. It also uses geometric cues only from the points and their local neighbors, so it cannot distinguish structures that are geometrically similar.

From these observations we get two critical questions: (1) Is geometry the only information we can use? (2) How can we use the geometric information from the points for matching? In practice humans find correspondences between objects by looking at global structures and local geometric cues. For example, to match an image to a point cloud as in Fig. 1, we first locate the building from its unique structure and then we identify the local structure of the roof for matching. Besides geometric cues, the visual context, like the color information at each point, also gives constraints for 2D-3D matching. This color information still preserves privacy, because the RGB data from sparse keypoints is not enough to reconstruct the scene.

Based on these observations and on GoMatch, we propose a new graph-based pipeline called DGC-GNN, which uses geometric and color cues in a global-to-local way for descriptor-free 2D-3D matching. DGC-GNN encodes the position and RGB information of each point and extracts a global distance-angular embedding that guides the local point matching. Inspired by earlier work, we use a cluster-based transformer to keep the information flow within local clusters. On real-world datasets we see that DGC-GNN gives large improvements in the number of correct matches and in pose estimation accuracy. It doubles the accuracy of GoMatch, so the gap between descriptor-based and descriptor-free methods gets smaller. Our paper makes the following contributions:

- We introduce a visual descriptor-free global-to-local GNN for direct 2D-3D keypoint matching. The network uses multiple cues and has a progressive clustering module to represent the keypoints. The pipeline makes sparse 2D-3D matching more accurate, and it needs low memory, preserves privacy, and has low cost for 3D model maintenance.

- We show that color information for each point is crucial for 2D-3D matching. When we add RGB encoding to our network, the performance improves significantly.

- Extensive experiments on real-world datasets show that DGC-GNN outperforms previous methods by a large margin on both matching and visual localization.

Besides geometric cues, visual context, such as the color information at each point, also provides constraints for 2D-3D matching. Importantly, this color information still preserves privacy, as the RGB data from sparse keypoints is insufficient to reconstruct the scene.

Building on these observations and on GoMatch, we propose a novel graph-based pipeline, named DGC-GNN, which leverages geometric and color cues in a global-to-local manner for descriptor-free 2D-3D matching. DGC-GNN encodes position and RGB information for each point and extracts a global distance-angular embedding to guide local point matching. Inspired by [19], we employ a cluster-based transformer to constrain information flow within local clusters. On real-world datasets, we observe that DGC-GNN leads to substantial improvements in both the number of correct matches and the accuracy of pose estimation. Notably, it doubles the accuracy of GoMatch, reducing the gap between descriptor-based and descriptor-free methods. In summary, our paper makes the following contributions:

- • We introduce a visual descriptor-free global-to-local GNN for direct 2D-3D keypoint matching. The network leverages multiple cues and incorporates a progressive clustering module to represent the keypoints. This pipeline improves the accuracy of sparse 2D-3D matching while requiring little memory, preserving privacy, and keeping the cost of 3D model maintenance low.

- • We demonstrate that the color information of each point is crucial for 2D-3D matching. Incorporating RGB encoding into our network yields significant performance improvements.

- • Extensive experiments on real-world datasets show that DGC-GNN outperforms previous methods by a large margin on both matching and visual localization tasks.
